justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias with gradual mean reversion toward a stable trend. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the last observed price level, assuming overnight conditions would not dramatically shift the underlying asset. The one-week estimate incorporates a slight upward drift consistent with recent momentum patterns, while the one-month estimate extends that drift further but with diminishing conviction, settling near a level that reflects a gentle continuation of the prevailing trend rather than any sharp acceleration or reversal.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the market has relatively little time to absorb new shocks, and liquidity conditions tend to dampen extreme intraday swings for most assets, keeping the range tight. By one week, macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and shifting sentiment can all introduce meaningful volatility. By one month, the range nearly doubles relative to the one-day interval because the cumulative effect of unknown future information — earnings surprises, geopolitical developments, policy shifts — becomes genuinely difficult to bound with high confidence.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as a hawkish policy surprise from a central bank, weaker-than-expected growth data, or a sudden credit event — could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices well above the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume relatively normal market functioning. Tail events — flash crashes, liquidity crises, or black swan shocks — are by definition poorly captured in any probabilistic interval, and real-world outcomes have historically demonstrated that even wide 90% confidence intervals are breached more frequently than the stated probability would suggest.
